posts.body_html:
Here's an exceptionally red throated clone that actually came from a rubricorpora mother plant! I culled everything else from the batch except this one, which stood out from the rest.

The name was actually stolen from my homie Mike Wilder: we were out in the field looking at plants many years ago, and he pointed to a rugelii and called it the eye of tron! I think that's in reference to an old ride at either disneyland or Disney world that was really tripped out, it was like you were riding right into the eye....of tron!

Anyways, just take a look at this darn thing! S. flava var. rugelii 'eye of tron' Liberty Co, FL, pics taken 6/7/23:






A newly opened trap, notice how light red the coloration is in comparison to the trap photographed above that has aged a bit:

posts.body_html:
Nice. I crossed F21 rubricorpora with F18 rugelii and got.... 50% rubricorporas and 50% rugeliis.

Anyone know why I didn't get any intermediates from this, as you would with a hybrid cross?

posts.body_html:
Jun 24, 2025 5:03:40 GMT -5 alexis said:
Nice. I crossed F21 rubricorpora with F18 rugelii and got.... 50% rubricorporas and 50% rugeliis.

Anyone know why I didn't get any intermediates from this, as you would with a hybrid cross?
If its dominant red coming from the Rubricorpora, and all offspring are not red, then we can assume the parent is Rr or heterozygous for dominant red. 

If the Rugelii is rr, then we are proposing a cross of Rr x rr, which will give you 50% Rr (red) and 50% rr (not red).

Of course this is theoretical and a best guesstimate, but it does fairly easily explain the results you are seeing from F21 x F18.

edit to add:  regarding intermediates... a red rugelii would just be a rubricorpora with a throat blotch, and a rubricorpora without the red is no longer a rubricorpora... so I expect you are seeing intermediates but phenotype wise they are segregating into red and not red.

-Dan
